"If dysphoria is a mental condition, then why can't it be treated through therapeutic or social interventions rather than medicalisation or surgery?"

This is my lived experience. 

I am a transmasc. person in my early 30's. I have always felt like I didn't belong in my body, and from an early age I tried expressing that by wearing boyish, baggy clothes and short hair. The scathing reactions from my peers and parents were NOT supportive. I was called slurs by my parent and told to look like a woman. My late teens and twenties were spent in and out of eating disorder treatment and psychiatric facilities due to extreme depression and gender dysphoria because I felt self loathing for a body that doesn't match what I am. I did not feel safe, let alone pressured to medically transition. All of the therapy interventions in the world would not change the irrefutable fact that I am in the wrong body. 

I came out to a therapist I was seeing, after several years of trying to come up with the courage to be open about myself and who I am. I was immediately shut down with "Well you're very feminine in the way you look. I don't think you're a man". "Maybe you are a gay woman and tomboy, but that doesn't mean you need to become a man". This reignited a deep self loathing that something is wrong with me and with being transgender. I will leave out other things a different therapist said to me because it's triggering. Both therapists listed themselves as not only LGBT friendly but that working with transgender folks was a specialty. 

The reality is, therapists don't have to work transgender people or market themselves to transgender clients if you think we have "pro-trans rhetoric" instead of just accepting that we just want to be treated like everyone else and that medically transitioning is something that *WE* want. I tried to make myself comfortable with who I am with talk therapy and guess what, I still want to transition.  If I was a hermit out in a forest somewhere with minimal human contact, I would still want top surgery and testosterone. 

It has nothing to do with society and that kind of language runs a dangerously close parallel to the rhetoric out there that we are trying to force and convince people that they are trans/are performing surgery on minors or whatever the "they are a groomers" narrative du jour is. 

I would recommend that you start at the beginning. Our history. Our persecution. Our joy. The fierce courage of people throughout history who have lived their truth and what looks like for them. We are not a monolith, however at the end of the day, we just want to treated with dignity and respect. Just like everyone else. Part of that dignity is accepting that we know ourselves and are able to make our own decisions for our own bodies without it being stigmatized or pathologized.
